title: 2027-11-01-meridian-care-failure-analysis-and-hardenings-workshop
summary: Post-incident workshop to review Friday's inference cascade affecting Meridian Care's inference endpoint. Discussed root causes (KV cache eviction + burst autoscale lag + misconfigured retry/backpressure), proposed mitigations (prefix caching, circuit breaker, autoscale tuning, canary rollback), and agreed next steps for bench tests and config changes. Action owners and tentative dates captured.
topics: Retry, circuit breaker, and rate limiting adjustments
action_items: Omar - collect and share GPU pod kube events + kv-cache eviction logs (due 2027-11-04)
Priya/Tom - provide list of critical routes and P95 latency SLOs (due 2027-11-03)
Maya - send updated pricing/commit impact for dedicated reserved capacity options (due 2027-11-05)
Liang - schedule follow-up bench test with Meridian test dataset and Redwood Optimize presets (target 2027-11-08)
Ayesha - run a small canary with reduced concurrency + new backpressure policy and report errors (due 2027-11-06)
next_steps: Redwood to run a focused benchmark reproducing the cascade with Meridian sample workload
Customer to open support ticket with full traces and KMS key usage logs
Joint canary test next week with rollback thresholds and extra observability hooks
questions: Can Redwood simulate the exact KV cache hit pattern we saw?
What's the recommended autoscale buffer for our p95 traffic spikes?
Does Redwood's Private offering change audit log availability for us?
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to run through the Friday cascade and make sure we have concrete mitigations. We have Daniel, Priya, Ayesha from Meridian, and I'll hand it to Omar to kick off the timeline.

[00:18] Omar Patel: Yeah thanks. Quick note first, I'm gonna probably mis-say some of the infra names, the firefly id that you used, sorry if I mix terms. So timeline as we saw: at ~10:14 UTC we saw gradual latency increase, by 10:20 p95 was up, 10:23 502 errors spiked as the KV prefix cache started evicting entries and the GPU pods couldn't warm KV sufficiently. There was also a burst in concurrent requests which hit the autoscaler hard.

[00:46] Priya Singh: Right and to add, the traffic shape was a multi-tenant spike — a partner campaign that overlapped with an internal job, so we had a lot of similar prefixes. I don't think we had misrouting but our prefix collision on the cache was higher than expected.

[01:07] Ayesha Khan: We saw retries amplify the tail. The app-layer retried 3 times with exponential backoff but because the underlying requests were timing out it thrash. We had circuit breaker rules but they were too loose.

[01:27] Daniel Ortega: Just to be super clear: this is the one that impacted production 2, correct? The one that's on the prod-dedicated group?

[01:33] Maya Chen: Yes, production cluster 2 — you're on Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity, right? We think autoscale and reserved pools interplay was part of the issue.

[01:45] Tom Becker: Quick question — was there any KMS latency contributing? We saw a handful of auth timeouts in the header of traces.

[01:54] Omar Patel: Good point. There were ~7 auth retries, some of that looks like KMS key access delays, perhaps caused by congestion on the HSM path. We're still correlating.

[02:11] Maya Chen: Ok let me walk through the proposed mitigations and then we can assign. First: increase prefix cache TTLs and change eviction policy to favor hot prefixes for 20 minutes for critical routes. Second: tune autoscale to pre-warm an extra N pods when rate of increase is above threshold — essentially a predictive upscaler. Third: tighten circuit breaker and add token bucket per-route. Fourth: short-term cadence: rollback the canary that rolled last week if it helps.

[02:46] Priya Singh: On TTLs — how do we avoid cache pollution if we extend TTLs? We saw prefix collisions. We don't want to keep stale cache entries for low-traffic tenants.

[02:57] Omar Patel: We recommend combining TTL with LRU per-prefix and a hot-list of customer routes that we pin. For low-volume tenants we would keep shorter TTLs. We'll need your list of critical routes to pin.

[03:17] Ayesha Khan: About autoscale, are you suggesting lowering the scale-out threshold or adding a predictive element? We worry about cost with overprovisioning.

[03:28] Maya Chen: Two-pronged: predictive warm-up (small buffer lets KV warm) plus a fast path for burst concurrency that leverages cached KV replicas. Redwood Optimize can simulate cost vs buffer tradeoffs; Liang will run that.

[03:43] Liang Wu: I'll capture that. We can run a sim using your recent two-week traffic to show cost delta at different buffers and also show expected p95 improvements.

[03:55] Tom Becker: Can we also get more granular tracing? The traces we have are a bit coarse — we need token-level timing so we can see KV lookup vs kernel times.

[04:05] Omar Patel: We can enable per-token telemetry for the bench. It does add overhead but it's fine for a short run. We'll send instrumentation steps.

[04:18] Daniel Ortega: I want to talk about retries and clients. The exponential backoff in our mobile clients was pretty aggressive. Is there a recommended client policy?

[04:26] Maya Chen: Yes, we recommend short backoff + jitter and client-side circuit breaking at lower thresholds than server. For tight latency SLOs, prefer failing fast with a graceful degrade to cached results.

[04:38] Ayesha Khan: Regarding security & audits — Meridian needs the audit artifact for the incident for SOC2. Can Redwood provide the full request traces and KMS access logs?

[04:47] Maya Chen: We can provide audit logs; for KMS access logs we will need cross-check with your key manager (if it's customer-managed) — but we can provide our side of the access logs and any Cloud HSM telemetry we have.

[04:59] Priya Singh: Also, Private deployment — would moving to Private give us more control over KMS latency?

[05:06] Omar Patel: Potentially, yes — Private lets you host the control plane in your VPC and keep KMS in-region/on-prem, which reduces third-party HSM network hops. But it comes with ops overhead.

[05:19] Tom Becker: Can we get a cost estimate for Dedicated reserved + Private delta?

[05:26] Maya Chen: I'll send a spreadsheet with cost delta and commit levels. Quick note — reserved Dedicated can reduce tail exposure because you control the pool size, but it doesn't fully eliminate cache warming issues.

[05:39] Daniel Ortega: Let's move through a tighter technical deep-dive: Omar, can you explain the KV cache eviction behavior and how it interacts with shard pinning?

[05:47] Omar Patel: Sure. So KV cache is sharded; eviction happens per-shard based on estimated memory pressure and an LRU-ish policy. When we have many similar prefixes the effective hot set grows and LRU starts thrashing, causing warm misses. Shard pinning prevents certain prefixes from being evicted but you need to pin with care; pinned prefixes consume memory. There's also async replication that can lag on heavy writes.

[06:15] Priya Singh: Is there an easy way to see per-prefix hit rates from the Redwood Console?

[06:22] Liang Wu: We have a per-prefix dashboard but it's not enabled by default for all customers due to telemetry cost. We can enable for a short period to diagnose.

[06:33] Ayesha Khan: We also noticed GPU pod churn when pods tried to come up and attach the KV state; there's a 12-18s cold start for some pods which allowed queueing. Can that be reduced?

[06:44] Omar Patel: Cold start is partly kernel init and model load; you can reduce it with quantized model variants or keep warm replicas. For the warm path we can preload KV with a small cache snapshot; Redwood supports snapshot restore on pod start.

[07:02] Tom Becker: That snapshot option — how consistent is it? We worry about staleness during writes.

[07:09] Omar Patel: Snapshots are eventual — we do a fast snapshot for hot prefixes, it's expected to be slightly stale for a few seconds depending on write QPS. For read-heavy routes it's fine.

[07:22] Priya Singh: Can you outline a short mitigation plan we can implement this week?

[07:28] Maya Chen: Yes: 1) Short-term (24-72h): tighten client retry & CB, pin top-50 prefixes, enable per-prefix telemetry, temporary autoscale buffer of +2 pods. 2) Mid-term (1-2 weeks): run Redwood Optimize bench, switch critical routes to longer TTLs with LRU hybrid, schedule canary with rollback thresholds. 3) Long-term: consider Private deployment for KMS and audit needs and reserved capacity purchase.

[07:58] Ayesha Khan: For the canary, what rollback thresholds do you suggest?

[08:03] Omar Patel: For this case, keep p95 < 350ms and error rate < 0.3% over 10 minutes window; if breached rollback. Also instrument token-level latencies.

[08:12] Daniel Ortega: Sounds reasonable. Can Redwood take responsibility for the bench reproduction? We need confidence before changing prod TTLs.

[08:18] Liang Wu: We'll run the bench using your anonymized traces; need a sanitized dataset and traffic envelope. I'll coordinate with Priya for data handoff.

[08:29] Priya Singh: We can sanitize and share by tomorrow EOD, but we need a secure upload URL.

[08:34] Maya Chen: We'll provide an S3 pre-signed or encrypted transfer and instructions.

[08:40] Tom Becker: One more question — did we see any sign that the fallback to smaller model variant was triggered? We thought the system might have auto-fallback enabled.

[08:48] Omar Patel: In the logs we didn't see automatic model fallback; we saw throughput shedding but not fallback. Fallback would have been recorded in the routing trace — we can double-check.

[08:58] Ayesha Khan: If we enable fallback next time, would that reduce error volume but maybe increase cost?

[09:03] Maya Chen: Exactly. Fallback reduces user-facing errors but sometimes increases token cost because smaller models still process some requests. It's a tradeoff. Redwood Console can show cost impact of fallback simulations.

[09:15] Daniel Ortega: Let's talk about compliance artifacts for SOC2. We need a timeline and the log package.

[09:21] Liang Wu: We'll prepare an export with request IDs, timestamps, and service-level metrics for the incident window. For KMS we'll include our access records; note that customer-managed keys will have separate logs.

[09:34] Priya Singh: Also include the rollout history and any config changes around TTL or autoscale from last two weeks.

[09:40] Maya Chen: We'll include that.

[09:45] Daniel Ortega: Okay, let's assign owners — Priya will provide routes + sanitized traces; Omar will gather infra logs; Liang will run bench; Maya will send commercial and next-steps.

[09:58] [crosstalk]

[10:03] Priya Singh: Quick ask — can Redwood provide a short runbook we can use internally for future cascade mitigation?

[10:09] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll share a 1-page runbook with step-by-step checks: 1) verify per-prefix hits, 2) escalate to canary rollback, 3) enable buffer, 4) open support case.

[10:20] Ayesha Khan: We'll expect that runbook and the pre-signed upload link.

[10:25] Maya Chen: Noted. Anything else?

[10:28] Daniel Ortega: One last thing — can we schedule a follow-up in 7 days to review bench results and a proposed canary window?

[10:34] Liang Wu: I'll set the calendar and include a dedicated 1-hour bench review.

[10:39] Maya Chen: Great. We'll reconvene after the bench; thanks everyone.

[10:45] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcription: some product names and acronyms may be slightly off (we heard "KV cache" sometimes transcribed as "K V cash") and speaker overlaps in the first 2 minutes.
